# V2 PART A — PRODUCT NORTH STAR AND IMMUTABLE ENGINEERING PRINCIPLES

## A1. Outcomes users should actually be able to demonstrate

1. **New user:** Install the app, view a fast cinematic **WELCOME TO J.A.R.V.I.S.** screen, tap official **Continue with Google**, authenticate with Google's supported identity flow, obtain a private J.A.R.V.I.S. account, select optional Google integrations, and enter the existing holographic assistant dashboard. If Google services are unavailable, show a clear, recoverable path rather than a broken loop.
2. **Existing user:** Upgrade in place without losing existing settings, chat history, memories, custom voice preferences, stored contacts aliases, or working Android features. Provide a secure, consented migration path when linking old local data to a Google identity.
3. **Android voice:** Say 'Hey JARVIS' during a supported active listening session. J.A.R.V.I.S. recognizes the spoken language, resolves pronouns and follow-ups, selects a valid action, asks for confirmation when needed, executes it, and speaks an accurate result. Include push-to-talk so the app remains useful where background wake words are constrained.
4. **Microphone-free computer:** Install the desktop companion. Pair with Android through a QR code/short-lived code and proof-of-possession exchange. On Android, say 'JARVIS, open Chrome on my Windows computer and search for ChatGPT'. The paired desktop launches the approved browser and navigates; Android receives the verified state and replies 'Chrome is open on your computer, and the search is ready.' Never claim success based solely on the language model's intention.
5. **Speaker-free computer:** Audio answers come from Android by default. Optionally relay supported desktop audio to Android, where the OS and user consent allow it. Not all desktop/system audio can be captured universally, and DRM-protected streams must be respected.
6. **Personal Google assistant:** Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, Contacts, YouTube, Classroom and other services are connected individually only when official APIs, account eligibility, scopes, and user consent permit it. Signing in with Google NEVER grants automatic access to all Google products. Distinguish connected API access from opening an app/web page.
7. **Low-end usable:** The essential home screen, voice control, call/contact actions, local commands, and pairing must work smoothly on compatible budget Android hardware. Use measured metrics rather than claims of 'zero latency' or 'perfect voice recognition'.
8. **Cross-platform installability:** Build Android APK/AAB, iOS signed IPA/TestFlight path, Windows EXE/MSI/MSIX where relevant, macOS signed/notarized DMG/PKG where configured, and Linux AppImage/deb/rpm where applicable. Produce actual installers only in environments with required toolchains and signing; otherwise leave reproducible CI and exact blockers.
9. **Intelligence you can test:** The 1,000 user requests and 2,000 example answers at the end are reproducible scenario/evaluation fixtures. They do not automatically 'train' or fine-tune a model. Build actual ASR benchmarks, tool-call tests, intent evaluation, agent simulations, memory tests, and human feedback loops.
10. **Futurism without fragility:** Cinematic animated core, holographic projections, responsive panels, 3D/orbital accents, context displays, system diagnostics, and refined feedback remain fluid, accessible, skippable, privacy-conscious, and power-efficient. No fake data panels.

## A2. Hard constraints: preserve all, promise no magic

- Never erase working functionality, rename package identifiers, rotate auth keys, or reset production data without an explicit migration and rollback plan.
- Classify every feature as IMPLEMENTED/VERIFIED, IMPLEMENTED/UNVERIFIED, PARTIAL, BLOCKED_BY_PLATFORM, BLOCKED_BY_PERMISSION, BLOCKED_BY_PROVIDER, NOT_STARTED, or EXPERIMENTAL. Never visually mark a nonfunctional demo as complete.
- Route every consequential action through typed tool schemas, authenticated identity, least-privilege capability checks, precondition validation, risk classification, optional user approval, execution, actual postcondition verification, and an auditable receipt.
- Never use arbitrary remote terminal execution as a default desktop feature. Use a narrowly scoped allowlist of safe built-in actions; explicit developer sandbox operations require independent consent and confinement.
- Never secretly monitor microphones, cameras, screens, messages, or other people. Display visible recording/sharing state; use session-scoped activation and OS-compliant foreground/service behavior; provide a one-tap stop.
- Never bypass Google sign-in consent screens, capture Google passwords, auto-authorize Gmail/Drive/Calendar, scrape locked account pages, or masquerade as official Google apps. Support granular OAuth permission denial and reauthorization.
- Never use the app to evade device security restrictions, elevation prompts, antivirus checks, age gates, or platform store protections. Explain legitimate alternatives.
- Never promise access to information that is not connected or available. Distinguish 'can't access', 'no results', 'disconnected', and 'permission denied'.
- Do not imply medical diagnosis, emergency-service guarantees, or therapy replacement from wellbeing features. Provide supportive breaks, accessibility, and optional routines without unhealthy tracking pressure.
- Design monetization, analytics, and account onboarding without deceptive UI, forced consent, insecure credentials, or dark patterns. Keep youth/minor accounts privacy-conscious.
- Use legally licensed or original voice, visual, audio, and model assets; offer local/offline modes without pretending free third-party inference is available by default.

## A3. Don't ask for endless clarifications — investigate and ship a thin slice

Inspect the actual repository, README, lockfiles, Gradle configs, Android manifests, mobile build configurations, package identifiers, existing backend endpoints, and CI. Choose the smallest compatible architecture change that delivers a real end-to-end test. If essential source code or credentials are unavailable, explicitly describe the blocker and create only the work that can be demonstrated. Do not generate blank repositories with dozens of pretend feature modules in place of upgrading the actual app.

# V2 PART B — DELIVERY ARCHITECTURE, PRECISELY DEFINED

## B1. Logical architecture

**Clients:** Android phone; optional iOS/iPadOS; Windows desktop companion/client; macOS companion/client; Linux companion/client; optionally web admin dashboard for authorized settings. Each client has an AccountService, PlatformCapabilityRegistry, CommandAdapter, ConnectionState, PrivacyControls, EncryptedLocalStore, and AccessibilityLayer.

**Identity:** Google Sign-In as primary first-launch sign-in using supported SDKs; verified identity token on backend; internal immutable user ID; server-side authenticated sessions; optional organization accounts and granular connections; token revocation; session/device management. Prefer platform-appropriate Credential Manager on Android; equivalent official sign-in on Apple/desktop. If Firebase Auth is already used, keep and harden it instead of replacing without reason.

**Shared backend:** Auth API, Session API, AI gateway, Tool Router, Memory Store, Connector Broker, Device Registry, Encrypted Pairing Service, Action Receipt Store, Realtime Transport Service, Notifications Scheduler, Feature Flag service, Cost Controls, Audit and Observability. Logical modules may share a deployable monolith, not necessarily independent microservices. Keep the simplest architecture adequate for the user base.

**Realtime protocol:** Authenticated WebSocket or documented equivalent; transport TLS; per-session user-bound authorization; short-lived pairing and device keys; replay protection; explicit target device; command ID/idempotency key; acknowledgement; progress; result receipt; timeouts; optional cancellation; reconnection; ordered dependent steps; and clear distinction between local-LAN and encrypted remote-relay modes.

**AI control plane:** Voice audio preprocessing and wake-word/VAD (where supported), speech-to-text, multilingual normalization, context resolver, task planner, typed tool selection, policy and permissions gate, user confirmation, execution, independent verification, answer composition, streaming text-to-speech. Model providers are configured through env-backed server adapters; offline compact models/ASR are optional based on device resources, licenses, and benchmarking.

**Data layer:** Account-scoped secure memory, conversations, device settings, personalized dictionary, contact aliases, tasks, reminders, evidence references, preference settings, connection metadata, receipts, usage and quota accounting. Encrypt sensitive material in transit and at rest, enforce server-side tenant isolation, log minimal operational metadata, and support export/deletion.

**Google connectors:** Identity credentials separate from Google API grants. Explicit scopes per operation; official API use only; least-privilege access; granular consent; reauth/revoke; quotas; API policy verification; 'can launch only' capability for unavailable APIs. Google Photos uses appropriately supported user selection flows, not imaginary all-library access. Protected password/security data never imported.

## B2. Repository structure (illustrative; adapt to source)

```
/apps/android/              Existing Android source, preserved and extended
/apps/ios/                  Native iOS target or cross-platform adapter when appropriate
/apps/desktop/              Windows/macOS/Linux companion
/apps/desktop-ui/           Optional common desktop shell and holographic dashboard
/backend/                   Secure APIs, auth, AI providers, sessions, tools
/packages/action-contracts/ Typed actions, result receipts, schemas, versioning
/packages/google-connectors/Official authorized integrations
/packages/device-protocol/  Pairing, capability negotiation, transport
/packages/evaluation/       Dataset, validators, regression runner
/packages/design-tokens/    Existing visual identity and accessible UI tokens
/docs/                      ADRs, permissions, install, privacy, release and tests
/.github/workflows/         Reproducible CI and platform builds
```

Preserve the existing repo layout if a restructure would break working builds. Add gradually behind stable interfaces, and write architecture decision records (ADRs) explaining important choices.

## B3. Platform decision rules

- **Android:** Prefer existing Kotlin/Java and Jetpack Compose if already used; preserve Android package and signing lineage. For app launching, intents and official OS APIs; for contacts use scoped permissions and nickname resolver; for calls use authorized supported dialing/calling APIs with appropriate confirmation; for system settings use sanctioned panels if direct writes are restricted. For voice be candid about Android background microphone/foreground service limitations. Android 9-class devices need a tested, reduced-resource mode where supported.
- **iOS:** Use SwiftUI/App Intents/Siri/Shortcuts and approved APIs, or existing React Native/Flutter target if legitimate reuse is possible; respect iOS background execution and app sandbox restrictions. Do not imitate system-wide arbitrary device control. Provide TestFlight/App Store release workflow with correct Apple signing requirements.
- **Windows:** Choose Tauri, Electron, .NET/WinUI, or existing suitable stack based on audited source. Desktop companion is visible to user, supports installed-app allowlist, file picker and scoped file operations, window focus/bring-to-front only where permitted, clipboard opt-in, capture consent, and optional supported audio loopback. Do not require built-in mic/speakers.
- **macOS:** App bundle with proper privacy entitlements and Accessibility/Screen Recording approvals for supported functions. Respect Gatekeeper, signing, notarization requirements, and app sandbox where applicable.
- **Linux:** Handle X11/Wayland limitations, application launch via desktop entries, PipeWire/portal permissions for screen/audio capture, distro packaging differences, and variable audio stacks. Never promise universal GUI automation on all compositors.

## B4. Secure phone-to-desktop command protocol (contract)

A normalized command must contain only validated data, not raw executable code:

```
ActionRequest {
  schema_version, command_id, requester_user_id,
  target_device_id, session_id, issued_at, expires_at,
  action_type, normalized_parameters,
  required_capabilities, risk_level, confirmation_token?,
  idempotency_key, correlation_id
}
ActionReceipt {
  command_id, target_device_id, accepted_at,
  started_at?, completed_at?, state,
  verified_postcondition?, safe_result_summary?,
  error_category?, retryable?, user_action_needed?
}
```

Allowed starter action types: desktop.open_app (verified installed app), desktop.open_url (validated http/https and approved handlers), desktop.focus_window (per OS permission), desktop.show_notification, desktop.search_files (selected authorized folders), desktop.open_file (scoped file), desktop.search_web, desktop.type_text_into_focused_app (explicit user foreground focus and OS-approved input method), desktop.read_screen_session (consent), device.get_status, and device.transfer_selected_file. Add other actions through reviewed schemas, dedicated adapters, risk analysis, test coverage and feature flags.

Pairing security: show a one-time QR or short code on the desktop; user confirms on phone and computer; exchange authenticated identities; store device-bound keys securely; set short pairing expiry; tie every device to the current user; display last active time and capabilities; allow unpair/revoke from both sides; support local-only transfer and an explicitly enabled secure relay when not on the same LAN. No internet-facing unprotected desktop port, default credentials, universal shared secret, or silent remote control.

Example verified state machine:

```
USER_SPEAKS -> PHONE_CAPTURES -> ASR_TRANSCRIBES -> INTENT_RESOLVES
-> DEVICE_SELECTED -> CAPABILITY_CHECK -> POLICY_CHECK
-> OPTIONAL_CONFIRMATION -> REQUEST_DISPATCHED
-> DESKTOP_ACKNOWLEDGES -> ACTION_EXECUTES -> POSTCONDITION_VERIFIED
-> RECEIPT_RETURNED -> ANDROID_SPEAKS_VERIFIED_RESULT
```

Recover from weak Wi-Fi, offline computer, invalid permissions, app not installed, failed launch, focus failure, multiple devices, lost receipt, and conflicting commands. Do not equate an acknowledgement with successful execution.

## B5. Microphone/audio design and performance

Use Android microphone as the voice input device when desktop lacks one. Offer push-to-talk plus supported explicitly activated listening; on-device VAD, gain normalization, echo cancellation when available, clipping detector, noise suppression; optional diarization only in consensual recordings; multilingual ASR; custom vocabulary; graceful confidence handling; barge-in interruption; TTS pacing and response chunking; Bluetooth routing; silence timers; visible mic indicator. Test with real phone hardware. Audio streaming should use appropriate codecs and transport where technically supported, and protect recordings from accidental retention.

Measure: wake-word false-activations/hour, miss rate, command intent accuracy, WER by environment/language, end-of-speech-to-first-text latency, end-of-speech-to-first-audio latency, audio underruns, CPU/GPU load, memory pressure, thermal/battery impact, disconnect recovery and accessibility. Set baseline goals after profiling; do not promise universal perfection, zero latency, perfect speech, or impossible non-consensual omnipresence.

For computer audio return, support only documented OS capture methods with explicit consent and copyright/DRM protections. Prioritize assistant TTS through Android; desktop general-audio relay is optional and must disclose platform limits.

## B6. Google first-launch UX and consent model

**First-launch exact journey:** Splash within performance budget -> animated WELCOME TO J.A.R.V.I.S. screen -> concise privacy explanation -> branded **Continue with Google** -> system-supported Google identity prompt -> backend verified ID token -> create/load private J.A.R.V.I.S. profile -> optional personalized greeting/language -> opt-in Google Connections Center -> existing home AI core and command bar. Returning users with valid session open home without repeated forced animation. Handle cancellations, denied access, offline network, revoked sessions, account switching, repeated sign-in, and user deletion.

**Personal assistant per person:** Stable internal user ID; account-scoped memories, chats, voice settings, languages, preferences, devices, contacts aliases, skills, app integrations, and automation recipes. Verified tenant isolation on every backend read/write. No Google password capture. OAuth consent for Gmail/Calendar/Drive/Photos/etc must be requested separately, at the time of use, with minimum scopes. Use official Google APIs or properly labeled app/web launch options. Some Google products expose no suitable direct API or are limited by account eligibility and verification. Show Connected / Permission Needed / Launch Only / Not Supported accurately.

**Google services panel:** Communication (Gmail/Contacts/Calendar/Tasks/Meet/Chat where permitted); documents (Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Forms); education (Classroom where eligible); search and knowledge (Search, Scholar, Translate, Maps, YouTube APIs, etc. where supported); cloud/dev (Firebase, Cloud, Colab, Apps Script as official portal or authorized API); media (YouTube, Photos Picker, compatible players); business (Analytics/Search Console/Business Profile only by authorized scopes); security/Wallet/Password Manager link-out ONLY. Use full Google service catalog appended later in this file; classify each entry honestly.

**Suggested wording:** 'Signing in gives J.A.R.V.I.S. your basic account identity. Choose which Google apps to connect next. You can skip this step and connect them later.' Never claim one-tap sign-in connects *every* Google product. For Gmail restricted scopes, follow official OAuth verification and any applicable independent security-assessment requirements before distributing publicly.

## B7. AI memory, safety and quality

Memory records should retain origin, consent, scope, TTL, confidence, timestamp and edit/delete controls. Use retrieval rather than infinitely stuffed prompt context. Isolate hypothetical examples from real-life facts. Let users correct memory. Record only task-relevant and authorized data. Use a transparent 'why do you know this' source view.

Every AI answer must separate verified observations from suggestions. Every action result must cite a tool receipt or fail honestly. Train/evaluate classification and voice accuracy using anonymized, consensual fixtures; the attached 1,000 / 2,000 examples are NOT an already trained model. High-stakes health, money, legal and safety topics should use cautious information, not unsupported guarantees or diagnosis. Make wellbeing prompts optional, nonintrusive and supportive of healthy use.

# V2 PART C — DEVELOPMENT PHASES WITH REPRODUCIBLE ACCEPTANCE GATES

**Phase 0 — Audit:** Identify actual technology stack, current app package, working source, dependencies, SDK and API levels, existing backend URL and 404 behavior, current storage, known crashes, assets, and signing. Create baseline screenshots and feature manifest. Do not wipe anything.

**Phase 1 — Working Android baseline:** Rebuild existing APK; ensure app launches on target hardware; resolve AI backend endpoint via a real health check and documented URLs; implement secure auth model; verify mic permission path, local commands, streaming response, and concise errors. Define safe token use and quotas.

**Phase 2 — Welcome + Google identities:** Build first-run welcome; official Sign in with Google; verified server sessions; account-scoped data and migration; user-specific assistants; opt-in connector dashboard; logout/delete/revoke. Test two-user data isolation and denied scopes.

**Phase 3 — First desktop companion:** Build one real desktop agent and a reproducible installer, normally Windows first. Pair via QR/code; support app launch, browser URL, window focus and verified receipts; demo phone mic -> desktop Chrome search -> phone TTS. Validate blocked/denied states, reconnection, replays, unpair, and no desktop audio hardware.

**Phase 4 — macOS/Linux adapters:** Provide legitimate native compatibility using their respective permissions, limitations and packaging. Keep a shared typed command contract. Produce platform-specific integration tests.

**Phase 5 — Voice precision:** Improve wake detection, noisy ASR, interruptions, custom vocabulary, language switching, TTS, acoustic diagnostics and Bluetooth support. Measure accuracy/latency by device, language and acoustic condition; never claim 'perfect'.

**Phase 6 — Core Google tools:** Add narrowly scoped Calendar/Tasks/Drive file picker/Docs/Sheets/Contacts as account policies allow; add Gmail after restricted-scope requirements are met. Build a live API capability directory; partial granular scope denial must not break unrelated integrations.

**Phase 7 — Memory + intelligence:** Durable scoped memory, explicit memory editing, project/workflow knowledge, research citations, reasoning checks, tool-call contracts, failure diagnosis, multi-model routing, offline simple commands, model cost controls. Regression-test natural conversation quality.

**Phase 8 — iOS companion:** Create real native-installable iOS client with proper Apple signing flow and App Intents/Shortcuts integrations where possible. Do not promise arbitrary remote control of unrelated iOS apps. Verify phone voice and existing account interoperability.

**Phase 9 — Holographic interaction upgrade:** Keep current visual identity, refine AI core, add meaningful animated states and reactive waveform, personalized home, modular status cards, polished controls, diagrams, accessible text and reduced motion. No visual redesign surprises or unverified metric displays.

**Phase 10 — Feature backlog implementation:** Tackle 1–1,500 as independently tracked epics/features with implementation + unit/integration/E2E test + documented constraints. Use risk-based priorities. Never create 1,500 empty buttons and mark the entire backlog done.

**Phase 11 — Evaluation:** Run the 1,000 utterance cases, 2,000 answer examples, new negative tests for Google scope denial, two-account isolation, desktop companion revocation, ASR accents/noise, offline mode, file and app permissions, and anti-hallucinated action receipts. Keep release-specific test artifacts.

**Phase 12 — Release:** Build Android APK/AAB, iOS IPA/TestFlight as signing allows, Windows EXE/MSI, macOS DMG/PKG as supported, and Linux release formats; provide CI pipelines and reproducible install instructions, privacy policy, notices, changelog, app icons, data safety disclosures, and staged rollout plan. Never falsely claim an installer has been built when code signing or toolchains are missing.

**Mandatory vertical-slice demo before adding breadth:** With Android microphone and Android speakers only, successfully say 'JARVIS, open Chrome on my paired computer and search for ChatGPT'; see the correct browser page on the computer, receive a signed/verifiable action receipt, and hear an accurate confirmation on the PHONE. If unavailable, state the exact error and recovery step.

## C2. Project repository output contract

Every development iteration must produce: (1) concise architecture decision, (2) changed files/commits, (3) verified build/test commands and results, (4) permission/security implications, (5) updated feature status rows, (6) demonstration instructions, (7) unresolved blockers, (8) next highest-value tasks. Work on actual source. Don't emit pseudo-code pretending to be a final app. Where tool access is limited, produce implementable code and state what couldn't be verified.

## C3. Per-feature quality checklist for the entire 1,500-item catalog

For EACH feature ID below, derive and maintain the following implementation record:

- **Intended user outcome:** one-sentence measurable behavior and the user scenario that triggers it.
- **Supported platform(s):** Android / iOS / Windows / macOS / Linux / server, with a reason if unavailable.
- **Interfaces and contracts:** screens, commands, action schemas, permissions/scopes, data fields, and error categories.
- **Execution path:** what runs locally, on the paired desktop, or via authorized backend and third parties.
- **Privacy and cost:** data touched, consent needed, local retention, rate limits, provider/API costs, and youth-appropriate safeguards.
- **Failure handling:** no device, denied permission, missing account, network loss, unsupported OS, stale data, wrong speech interpretation, user cancellation.
- **Acceptance test:** exact given/when/then test using real or documented mocked inputs; test no unauthorized action and no fake success.
- **Performance:** measurable latency, CPU/RAM, energy or network metric relevant to that feature.
- **Shipping status:** NOT_STARTED / PARTIAL / TESTED / BLOCKED / SHIPPED backed by evidence, not marketing claims.

**Implementation discipline:** Do not use huge context windows as a substitute for this feature registry. Break backlog into modules and staged PRs, but maintain the full registry as the unabridged source of truth. No feature may be quietly removed because it is difficult, though a feature may be marked blocked with supported reasons.

4. Treat the following as design priorities, not assumed verified facts: low-end/mid-range Android compatibility (including Redmi 9-class phones), reliable microphone/voice state transitions, a correct secure backend URL, a clearly optional **client/session token** distinct from an AI-provider API key, fast response to basic commands, modern animated UI, and multilingual English/Spanish/Persian support.
5. The initial backend problem to solve is connectivity: an HTTP **404** often means the route/path or deployed function is wrong, not that the AI is incapable of answering. Design diagnostics that separately distinguish wrong hostname, missing route, invalid method, failed authentication, rate limits, missing provider configuration, timeouts, and offline state. Do not ask users to guess backend URLs.
6. Never invent unsupported Android powers. When a capability cannot be delivered due to Android version, manufacturer, device hardware, runtime permission, app sandbox, missing third-party API, regional service, or store policy, show a disabled/limited state with a **real alternative** and document it in the feature matrix. Specifically do not use AccessibilityService as an unrestricted autonomous agent or to evade device security controls.
7. All 300 requirements must be tracked using feature IDs 001–300 in an auditable feature registry with status: **implemented and tested, implemented with limitation, behind experiment flag, specified for a future milestone, or blocked with reason**. Do not mark a placeholder as implemented. A realistic staged delivery is preferable to a fictitious claim that everything works in one build.
8. Provide the complete code, backend, configuration examples, migrations, documentation, test fixtures, deployment scripts, and release checklist possible in the available workspace. If the tool cannot output everything at once, prioritize a functioning baseline and continue in coherent, fully executable modules; never return only a vague plan where actual source can be created.

### B. PRODUCT QUALITY TARGETS — MEASURE, DO NOT FABRICATE RESULTS
- **First render:** usable interface immediately; target under approximately 1.5 seconds on a tested baseline device where feasible. Measure cold/warm starts instead of promising a universal time.
- **Simple offline actions:** target immediate response, normally within hundreds of milliseconds on supported phones. No mandatory cloud call to read local battery or open installed applications.
- **Online voice:** minimize wake-to-transcript and transcript-to-first-audio; target a fast perceived start, with explicit streaming and honest failure status. Report measured p50/p95 latency by device and network.
- **Reliability:** no crashes during happy-path workflows; run automated suites, stress runs, and physical-device tests. Make error recovery visible and recoverable.
- **Visual quality:** original cinematic cyan/blue/charcoal HUD with restrained gold/white highlights; readable, precise, and fast. Provide Minimal and Reduced-Motion fallbacks.
- **User well-being:** no manipulative engagement loops, no emotionally dependent AI persona, no excessive alerts, no unrequested voice capture, quiet hours, accessible controls, age-appropriate defaults, and transparent AI limitations.
- **Battery/thermal health:** avoid unnecessary always-on CPU and background microphone usage, observe platform lifecycle restrictions, limit network/battery cost, adapt effects, and show usage controls.
- **Security:** server-side provider secrets, principle of least privilege, explicit consent for sensitive actions, audited tool calls, encrypted sensitive storage, authentication, quotas, and trustworthy error messages.
- **Cost:** model routing, usage budgets, cache where safe, user-visible AI cost summaries, and safe handling when budgets are exhausted.
- **Language:** English, Ecuadorian-friendly Spanish, and Persian with correct RTL, transcription, pronunciation, and language-specific fonts that are legitimately licensed and bundled only if allowed.

### C. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE — REQUIRED MODULES
Implement a maintainable modular client/server architecture. Prefer **Kotlin + Jetpack Compose** and stable compatible AndroidX libraries for Android, using clean layers `ui -> ViewModel -> domain/use-case -> repositories -> local/remote data`. Use Kotlin coroutines/Flow for streams, lifecycle-aware Compose state, Navigation Compose, Room for structured local storage, DataStore for settings, Android Keystore for appropriate key protection, and WorkManager for deferrable background work. Hilt or a comparably testable dependency-injection approach is fine. Use CameraX for permitted camera sessions, ML Kit or another verified OCR solution for local extraction, official Android intents/providers for controls, NotificationListenerService only when opt-in and genuinely needed, and ARCore only when the device supports it. Do not introduce privileged services, rooted-device dependencies, or undocumented system toggles.

Build a **secure server** using a suitable TypeScript/Node framework that deploys to Vercel or an equivalent supported host. Separate request authentication, model-provider adapters, tool registry, input validation, authorization policy, persistence, observability, and streaming adapters. Use Postgres or similarly suitable managed storage for authenticated accounts/projects, a vector index only when it materially improves retrieval, an ephemeral cache/rate limiter where needed, and a task queue or scheduler for durable workflows. Never place provider secrets in Android assets, generated JavaScript bundles, URLs, Git history, public logs, or client tokens. Provide `env.example` with placeholders and private environment variable setup instructions.

Example repository architecture, adapt to the actual project:

```text

    core/common/                 # Result types, errors, logging redaction
    core/ai/                     # orchestration and model-independent request types

  backend/
```

**Dependency contracts:** Every feature registers its inputs, outputs, tool calls, state machine transitions, Android permission requirements, privacy sensitivity, success/failure feedback, availability, and acceptance tests. Prefer typed interfaces/serializers over free-form magic JSON. All components should compile, load, and gracefully degrade when optional dependencies are unconfigured.

### D. CORE AI AND COMMAND PROCESSING PIPELINE
1. Accept text, tapped command, speech transcript, authorized image/file, NFC trigger, or user-approved event as a **typed IntentRequest**.
2. Generate a request ID, detect locale, classify user intent, inspect privacy/permission scope, and route obvious local actions to deterministic handlers with no AI API request.
3. For general questions, retrieve bounded recent conversation context, user-approved relevant memories, available tool capabilities, and any explicitly selected file context.
4. Select a real configured AI model based on request complexity, required modalities, budget, and availability. Do not make up "ChatGPT version 15" or nonexistent provider model IDs.
5. Produce user-visible streaming text and proposed structured tool calls. Treat all model-produced tool requests as untrusted proposals until server and Android authorization policies approve them.
6. For externally consequential actions, present a human-readable **Action Preview** with destination, data fields, costs, undoability, and permissions; then wait for explicit user approval.
7. Execute through a typed tool adapter with idempotency keys and timeouts; deliver a real tool result or transparent failure. Never pretend an unexecuted call, message, or update succeeded.
8. Persist a minimal redacted execution receipt if the user has enabled action history, update conversation state, and keep memory extraction strictly opt-in.
9. Support `cancel`, `stop speech`, `undo` when possible, retries only for safe/idempotent actions, low-power mode, offline fallback, and accessible screen-reader states.

**Intent taxonomy:** `LOCAL_READ`, `LOCAL_ACTION`, `AI_CHAT`, `AI_RESEARCH`, `DOCUMENT`, `VISUAL`, `CONTACT`, `COMMUNICATION`, `SCHEDULE`, `AUTOMATION`, `DEVELOPER`, `AGENT_WORKFLOW`, `PRIVACY_CONTROL`, `DEVICE_SETTING`, `SYSTEM_ERROR`.

**Risk tiers:**
- Tier 0: local reads with prior permission and ordinary UI changes. Execute with immediate feedback.
- Tier 1: low-risk local actions such as opening a chosen app or starting a local timer. User initiated, reversible where possible.
- Tier 2: external communication, calendar writes, location sharing, changing device settings, publishing project changes, or syncing private data. Show a preview and require explicit approval.
- Tier 3: deleting data, account removal, financial/API spending beyond configured budgets, or other highly consequential actions. Show stronger warning, confirmation and/or device authentication as appropriate; never auto-execute.
- Unsupported: show why an action cannot run, give compliant alternatives, and never bypass platform restrictions.

### E. VOICE LOOP — FROM "HEY JARVIS" TO A REAL RESULT
Create a typed state machine:
`DISABLED -> IDLE -> WAKE_DETECTED -> LISTENING -> TRANSCRIBING -> ROUTING -> THINKING/TOOL_PENDING -> SPEAKING -> FOLLOW_UP_WINDOW -> IDLE`, with error, canceled, muted, and permission-denied states.
- Show persistent, honest microphone indicators and stop controls. Explain that Android may restrict background listening and microphone foreground services. Request `RECORD_AUDIO` only when an audio feature is activated. Do not start forbidden microphone services at boot or without a user-visible eligible entry point.
- Support on-device wake-word detection when feasible, tap-to-talk always, a selectable STT engine, local VAD, pause detection, voice interruption, streaming text and TTS, and Bluetooth headset routing where permitted.
- The approved wake greeting can be: **"Hello, sir. How can I help you?"** After activation, do not repeat it on every follow-up. Provide text-only alternative, quiet mode, and a single-stop control.
- Let users choose the session duration and whether follow-up listening is enabled; do not store raw audio by default. Voice samples must never be used as sole authentication for protected operations.
- Recognize natural speech such as: "Hey JARVIS, call My Dad", "Open YouTube", "How much battery have I got?", "Set a reminder for tomorrow at six", and "Why does my backend return HTTP 404?" Resolve exact contacts before initiating the standard call flow.

### F. BACKEND URL AND CLIENT TOKEN — NO MORE AMBIGUOUS 404 ERRORS
The Android Settings screen MUST distinguish:
- **Backend Base URL**: e.g. `https://YOUR-PROJECT.vercel.app` (hostname only; do not double-append `/api`).
- **Health Endpoint**: auto-derived `GET /api/health`.
- **Assistant Endpoint**: auto-derived `POST /api/assistant/stream`.
- **Optional App Authentication**: short-lived user/session token or explicit pairing credentials (if the backend enforces them). The client token is NEVER a provider key, and a plain static token embedded in a distributed APK must NEVER be treated as a private secret.
- **AI Provider Configuration**: stored only in backend private environment variables, such as `AI_PROVIDER_API_KEY`, `DATABASE_URL`, and appropriate server-auth secrets. Configurable model IDs remain on the backend.

Backend acceptance contracts (adapt to real providers):

```http
GET /api/health
200 application/json
{"status":"ok","app":"JARVIS","version":"15.0","aiConfigured":true,"timestamp":"ISO-8601"}
```

`aiConfigured` is a coarse status, not a leak of provider names or secret values. Health must have a clear restricted variant if required by auth policy.

```http
POST /api/assistant/stream
Authorization: Bearer <short-lived-user-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "conversationId": "conv_123",
  "requestId": "unique-uuid",
  "locale": "en",
  "message": {"type": "text", "text": "What are you?"},
  "deviceCapabilities": ["battery_read", "open_app"],
  "clientVersion": "15.0"
}
```

Stream **well-defined, versioned SSE** events such as `response.started`, `response.text.delta`, `response.tool.proposed`, `response.tool.result`, `response.completed`, and `response.error`, each with a request ID and JSON payload. Permit client cancellation; honor auth, rate limits, safe tool argument validation, and structured failures. Provide a non-streaming fallback for devices/networks where streaming fails. Never fabricate `200 OK` when the provider request failed.

Diagnostic UI must include a **Test Connection** action displaying (1) DNS/TLS result, (2) endpoint HTTP status, (3) authentication status, (4) server provider configuration result, (5) a small authorized AI echo test, and (6) concise next steps. Typical errors: 404 wrong route, 405 wrong method, 401/403 auth, 429 usage limit, 500 backend bug, 502/503 provider/downstream, network timeout/offline, malformed payload. Mask private tokens in logs and screenshots.

### G. ANDROID PERMISSION AND STORE POLICY COMPLIANCE
- Choose current Google Play target SDK policy at build/release time. At the date of this specification, standard new Android apps/updates require Android 16/API 36 or later for Google Play submission. Keep `minSdk` low enough for the actual target devices where dependencies allow; do not raise minSdk casually. Validate target/compile compatibility and Play policy before release.
- **Calling:** prefer `ACTION_DIAL` showing the actual number, contact name, and SIM choice when relevant. `ACTION_CALL` requires its proper permission and user-initiated behavior; never simulate hidden phone calls. Do not automatically record calls.
- **Contacts:** runtime `READ_CONTACTS` only if used; consider contact picker to reduce permission scope. Names and numbers must not be uploaded unless separately approved for a purpose.
- **Messages:** use supported SMS, share, notification reply, or official provider APIs; no hidden message dispatch or unrestricted access to third-party app databases.
- **Notifications:** notification listener is sensitive; prominent opt-in, per-app filters, local redaction, and revocation instructions.
- **System settings:** use official settings panels or sanctioned APIs; no fake claims of toggling restricted Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or privacy states.
- **Overlay:** optional, clear purpose, close affordance, not a phishing or accessibility obstacle.
- **Camera/location/microphone:** foreground use, runtime consent, clear active indicators, stopped when session ends, with background restrictions obeyed.
- **Accessibility:** build a screen-reader-friendly UI, but do not misuse AccessibilityService for autonomous all-app control. Prefer narrow official intents and APIs.
- **Storage:** use scoped storage, Android Photo Picker and Storage Access Framework; do not demand unrestricted file access.
- **Background tasks:** prefer WorkManager for deferred work, scheduler/queue for cloud tasks, platform-compliant foreground service types only where eligible, and do not claim guaranteed continuous background listening.
- **Play Store and privacy:** supply privacy policy, accurate Data Safety declarations, account/data deletion, licensing review, permission justifications, export compliance, and an age-appropriate experience. If brand/IP questions arise about "JARVIS", check use rights before public branding.

### H. MEMORY, DOCUMENTS, SEARCH, AND AGENTS
- Separate chat history, saved personal memory, project knowledge, temporary session context, file embeddings, and third-party app data. Do not use a single unprotected pile of context for every task.
- Memory write flow: candidate fact -> source attribution -> privacy classification -> optional user confirmation or explicit opt-in setting -> encrypted storage -> retrieval relevance filters -> correction/deletion and TTL.
- Documents: user-chosen imports -> parse/OCR -> chunk -> index -> cite document/page -> controlled retention -> deletion from primary index and cache; never hallucinate having read an inaccessible file.
- Web research: use reliable search tool or user-configured connector, track sources and dates, treat all retrieved text as untrusted, and display clickable citations. Never expose tool credentials.
- Agents: coordination, research, code, planning, and execution agents may collaborate internally; every real-world action goes through deterministic authorization. Bound task duration, budget, tool scope, and completion criteria. Use asynchronous server jobs only with an actual scheduler/queue, never claim background work based on a local timer that Android may kill.
- Use narrow OAuth authorization for Gmail, calendars, GitHub, cloud storage, and third-party integrations. Explain connection requirements rather than assuming access exists. External send/edit/deploy actions require approval.

### I. UI/UX SYSTEM — ORIGINAL FUTURISTIC, NOT A STATIC SCREENSHOT
Design an original, elegant, functional sci-fi environment. Palette: near-black/space navy backgrounds, luminous cyan/azure accents, subtle electric-blue depth, carefully limited warm accent color for warnings or important actions. Typography: clean readable sans-serif + optional licensed technical display font for headings, not tiny decorative labels. Information density must be controlled on small screens. Use token-based layouts, reusable elements, responsive constraints, night mode, full TalkBack support, reduced motion, and contrast-safe text.

**Core visual primitive:** a central three-dimensional-feeling AI core made with lightweight Compose rendering: layered circles, glass-like ring highlights, controlled rotation, sound-driven waveform, soft glow, small orbital nodes. It changes color/motion accurately based on Idle, Listening, Interpreting, Thinking, Tool Awaiting Approval, Speaking, Offline, and Error. Provide a static minimal alternative. Do not run expensive 3D shaders continuously in the background. The core must actually respond to app state, not random cinematic loops.

**Essential interactive screens and routes:**
1. **First-run onboarding:** language choice, privacy summary, permissions on demand, server connection test, quick local demo, skip/return options.
2. **Home Command Core:** animated orb, tap-to-talk, text input, recent approved actions, time/date, battery/network, customizable modules, swipe/shortcut navigation.
3. **Live Voice Session:** realtime captions, input/output waveform, stop/pause/mute, transcript correction, voice route and quiet controls.
4. **Conversations:** streaming chat, source cards, action approval, edit/retry, image/file attachments, branches, export/delete.
5. **Command Palette:** instant searchable commands, argument preview, device availability, keyboard access, history.
6. **Device Hub:** battery, storage, CPU/thermal indicators where available, connection status, local controls, maintenance advice.
7. **Contacts and Calls:** permission explanation, search/aliases, disambiguation, prominent number preview, dial button, safe cancellation.
8. **Notifications and Messages:** opt-in listener, source badges, selected summaries, approved replies, privacy filters.
9. **Calendar and Tasks:** day/week views, reminders, priority, focus schedule, source integrations, editable event details.
10. **Student Workspace:** subjects, lessons, flashcards, assignment planner, research citations, tutor interactions.
11. **Developer Lab:** repository/context picker, Logcat interpreter, API health test, errors, tests, release checklist, sandbox for proposed changes.
12. **Research Center:** search results, evidence, source date, citation organizer, credibility and freshness indicators.
13. **Document Studio:** scanner, OCR, file list, page citation panel, document-grounded chat and deletion.
14. **Vision Camera:** explicit camera session, capture, viewfinder, overlays, safe image analysis, stop button.
15. **AR Experiments:** conditional hardware support test, clear camera permission, lightweight overlay demo, 2D fallback.
16. **Creative Studio:** original melody notes, storyboard cards, captions, thumbnails, brand rules, speech rehearsal.
17. **Travel and Location:** selected destinations, route alternatives, user-approved geofence reminders, weather, departure suggestions.
18. **Automations:** templates, natural-language builder, graph steps, test/dry-run, explicit consent, stop and undo labels.
19. **Agents and Mission Control:** delegated subtasks, status, remaining budget, citations, approvals, receipts, cancel controls.
20. **Memory Vault:** searchable fact cards, provenance, expiration, export, edit, deletion, global disable.
21. **Profiles and Themes:** visual variants, assistant personality, voices, language, custom shortcuts.
22. **Security and Privacy:** active sessions, permissions, app connections, retention rules, audit trail, delete/export.
23. **System Status:** online/offline mode, API status, current latency, quota, error explanations, network diagnostics.
24. **Backend Settings:** base URL editor, health test, auth connection, provider status (never show actual provider secret).
25. **Developer Options:** detailed redacted logs, feature flags, fake-device test scenarios, FPS/CPU/memory benchmarks.
26. **Updates and About:** build/versionCode, release notes, support, privacy policy, open-source acknowledgments.

Every screen must have loading, empty, disconnected, permission denied, stale-data, success, error, and retry states. Every control must perform a real action. No invisible or inert buttons. Use semantic content descriptions and avoid relying on color alone for status.

### J. A REPEATABLE SIX-STEP IMPLEMENTATION CONTRACT FOR ALL 300 FEATURES
For EACH numbered feature below, the assistant building this app MUST execute and document these six steps, not merely draw a screen:
1. **Contract:** define intended user value, user entry point, supported devices, required permissions, inputs, outputs, failure states, privacy scope, and risk tier.
2. **UI:** create a real accessible screen/card/control, including helpful empty, loading, success, permission-denied, and error states.
3. **Engine:** build Kotlin domain use-case and repository, connect official Android APIs or a real backend capability, and use typed schemas. Separate simulated/demo behavior from real operations.
4. **Safety:** use permission just-in-time, approval for impactful actions, data minimization, no hidden monitoring, explicit cost disclosure, and correct Android/store policy.
5. **Test:** add unit/integration/UI tests, physical device tests for hardware-dependent features, error injection, performance instrumentation, and clear pass/fail evidence.
6. **Release status:** mark implemented, limited, experimental, planned, or blocked with reason, and provide fallback alternatives and future dependencies. This six-step method applies to every item 001–300 even where individual entries below add more specific rules.

### K. COMPLETE FEATURE SPECIFICATION — ALL 300 REQUIREMENTS, NOTHING OMITTED

Below, every line states the requested capability, a concrete build instruction, and an acceptance test. **Keep the feature number stable in code comments, tickets, documents, and QA.** Do not delete duplicates just because two features share infrastructure; implement them as separate discoverable user capabilities reusing the same underlying modules.

# PART I — THE DEFINING J.A.R.V.I.S. 15.1 CROSS-DEVICE EXPERIENCE

## 1.1 Non-negotiable end-user story: no microphone or speakers in the computer
The primary user sits at a Windows, macOS, or Linux computer whose monitor works but which has no attached audio input or output. The user holds an Android phone with J.A.R.V.I.S. installed. A signed desktop companion named `Jarvis Desktop Bridge` is installed on that computer. On first run, the desktop displays an obvious "Pair with phone" QR code or human-readable one-time code. The Android app scans or types this code, verifies the desktop identity, and accepts a limited set of permissions. The desktop shows that this specific mobile device is paired. The user says into the Android phone: "Hey JARVIS, open Chrome on my computer and search ChatGPT." A local parser determines that the target is the selected computer. The desktop bridge receives the signed, authorized command, opens the selected browser or the system default browser, navigates to an encoded search URL, and confirms through a structured result that the launch and navigation request were accepted. J.A.R.V.I.S. then speaks through the PHONE: "I opened the browser and started a search for ChatGPT on your computer." If there is no verified navigation outcome, it says exactly what succeeded and what did not. The computer needs no microphone, no speaker, no driver hack, and no external audio hardware.

The same flow must work with spoken and typed commands. The user may ask: "On my Linux laptop, open the downloads folder"; "On my Mac, show the calendar"; "On the Windows desktop, open VS Code for my selected project"; "Pause the music on the connected computer"; "Find the PDF I saved in the shared study folder"; "Summarize my last build error"; "Show me the active app"; or "Tell me whether my other computer is online." Each command uses OS-specific, registered, typed operations. Unsupported operations show an honest error or official settings guidance, not a pretend success. If multiple computers are online, use a chosen default device, explicit device names, and a confirmation prompt on ambiguous requests.

### Minimum working demo acceptance criteria
1. Install Android app, install desktop companion on Windows, pair them without any microphone/speaker on Windows, and issue a tap-to-talk command.
2. Device opens browser to a search for an unambiguous user-supplied phrase, and phone audibly confirms the result.
3. Repeat with typed command and with a disconnected phone Wi-Fi then appropriate network/fallback error.
4. Revoke device pairing from desktop and prove previous phone cannot reconnect using cached credentials.
5. Execute safe file browsing in an explicitly granted folder, showing only file names until the user approves opening content.
6. Reject unknown actions, oversized messages, unpaired devices, expired commands, unauthenticated network traffic, and duplicated requests.
7. Continue to work if desktop audio input/output lists are empty and verify phone mic/speaker still function.
8. Demonstrate Android voice interruption, user-controlled microphone stop, and reduced-motion UI without lost commands.
9. On each OS, verify app launching and URL opening using native integration, not elevated shell access.
10. Record traceable, privacy-redacted command receipts and test user-visible failures.

## 1.2 Recommended three-tier architecture
**Tier A — Voice and control client on Android:** microphone capture, locally enabled wake-word model if supported, VAD, speech recognition, language identification, conversation screen, device picker, command preview, voice response via phone, opt-in session state, memory controls, local offline command classification, encrypted device identity keys, pairing wizard, and durable queue with expiry. Android does not need to emulate itself as a USB microphone for the computer: it exchanges structured commands directly. Avoid requiring new audio input hardware on the desktop.

**Tier B — Desktop Bridge on Windows/macOS/Linux:** signed native-installable application with visible tray/menu-bar status; user login session association; device inventory, allowlisted tool adapters, OS-specific launchers and accessibility integrations; browser URL opening; scoped file operations; job receipt publisher; local consent UI; automatic version update with signature verification; kill switch; event loop; reconnect/backoff; and readable diagnostics. It is neither a backdoor nor a silent monitoring tool. It never installs as root/admin by default and does not run commands with privileges the signed-in user does not already have. For graphical operations it may need to be running in the user's unlocked graphical desktop session.

**Tier C — Optional cloud AI and relay:** secure backend supplies model access, user-authenticated sync, optional account linking, end-to-end device rendezvous and delivery when direct LAN is not possible, rate limiting, revocation, event receipts, and push notifications. The relay never grants remote execution merely because the request text sounds confident. In offline local mode, Android and Desktop Bridge can speak over the same local network after authenticated pairing; local intent grammar handles supported commands without any external model key. True broad open-domain AI needs an actual local model, remote model, or a user-configured inference endpoint. Do not misrepresent this reality.

### Monorepo target, modify existing repo rather than starting over
```text
jarvis-15.1/
  apps/android/                  Kotlin/Compose unless audited source dictates otherwise
  apps/ios/                      optional native SwiftUI or proven cross-platform equivalent
  apps/desktop/                  Tauri 2, Electron or native shell chosen from repo audit
  packages/protocol/             JSON-schema, protobuf or typed cross-platform contracts
  packages/intent-catalog/       action names, entities, permissions, risk, tests
  packages/voice/                VAD/STT/TTS adapters and quality tests
  packages/ai/                   provider-neutral, local model abstraction, safe tool planning
  packages/design-system/        motion tokens, state-driven HUD, accessibility rules
  packages/localization/         English, Spanish, Persian; pronunciation dictionaries
  services/api/                  identity, cloud model proxy, optional sync, relay
  services/relay/                optional authenticated encrypted device transport
  data/training/                 1000 utterances, 2000 example responses, eval manifest
  docs/                           architecture, pairing, threat model, installers
  .github/workflows/             Android CI, Windows/macOS/Linux installer builds
  tests/                          unit, integration, contract, security, OS smoke tests
```

## 1.3 The two communication modes
**Local LAN direct mode (first priority):** Desktop Bridge advertises only non-sensitive service metadata using mDNS/Bonjour/Zeroconf or an approved manual IP/hostname fallback. Discovery is not authorization. Initiate a challenge-response pairing through a QR carrying only one-time session metadata, endpoint and public key fingerprint. Establish a mutually authenticated encrypted session, bind the phone key to desktop key, and show both device names. The bridge must not accept arbitrary HTTP commands just because traffic comes from a private IP. Use mature authenticated cryptographic libraries; prefer transport libraries such as TLS 1.3 with appropriate certificate identity verification rather than inventing encryption. Pairing keys go in Android Keystore and native OS secure storage. Do not embed fixed credentials in distributed builds. Rotate/revoke keys and support fresh pairing after device loss.

**Optional off-LAN mode:** Only after a separate explicit opt-in, route through authenticated cloud relay or VPN-like user-controlled connectivity. Treat desktop actions as privileged even if transport is authenticated. Implement per-device capability grants, durable asynchronous jobs with expiration and receipts, replay prevention, request quotas, connection presence and clear activity indicators. The user may disable internet remote control entirely while leaving local LAN mode enabled. Never suggest opening an unauthenticated local web server to the public internet, unsafe port-forwarding, or exposing a raw shell. No unrestricted remote desktop by default. Remote screen sharing, if added, requires separate on-device approval and appropriate native portals.

**No-key baseline:** Desktop launcher, safe URL navigation, known folder opening, local status reporting, timers, user-entered commands, pairing, and protocol heartbeats can work without commercial AI keys on a shared LAN. Offline speech recognition and TTS depend on compatible installed on-device models and resource constraints. Complex research, live search, weather, cloud translation and provider-powered AI require configured APIs or alternate accessible providers; each feature must display its current availability.

## 1.4 Pairing protocol with human-readable UX
State machine: `NOT_INSTALLED -> BRIDGE_STARTED -> PAIRING_ADVERTISED -> CODE_SCANNED -> MUTUAL_AUTH -> CAPABILITY_REVIEW -> PAIRED -> CONNECTED -> LIMITED / OFFLINE -> REVOKED`. Show device identity, OS, last connection, granted scopes and whether internet relay is enabled. Expire a QR/session code rapidly; bind it to an authenticated desktop-created pairing attempt; do not allow silent pairing from traffic on the LAN. Require a matching confirmation phrase/code displayed on BOTH devices for trust establishment. Implement rate limits and brute-force resistance for pairing attempts. Show explicit scopes: launch apps, open links, read selected folder metadata, manipulate selected files, adjust permitted media playback, show active window title, optional GUI automation. No scope should imply "read everything" or "take over the device". Separate dangerous operations into stronger consent categories. Pairing a device does not authorize every future action or permanent microphone capture.

The Android pairing screen shows steps: 1) install bridge from a verified release; 2) open bridge and choose pair; 3) scan displayed code; 4) compare verification code; 5) choose allowed capabilities; 6) try a safe ping and open-browser test; 7) pick default device and fallback voice output. The desktop shows a persistent device list, revoke button, suspend all remote actions, and an active session indicator. Add convenient QR display in settings and a manual one-time code alternative for cameras that do not work. Support no local discovery due to Windows firewall, macOS local-network permission or Linux mDNS failures; show specific fix steps without requesting firewall deactivation or running as admin unnecessarily.

## 1.5 Command protocol design
A command is typed data rather than arbitrary agent-generated code. Suggested request body:
```json
{
  "protocol_version": "1.0",
  "request_id": "uuid",
  "timestamp_ms": 0,
  "expires_at_ms": 0,
  "origin_device_id": "paired-phone-id",
  "target_device_id": "paired-desktop-id",
  "user_intent": "OPEN_WEB_SEARCH",
  "arguments": {"query": "ChatGPT", "browser": "system_default"},
  "capability_scope": "browser.open_search",
  "idempotency_key": "unique-operation-token",
  "requires_confirmation": false
}
```
Use canonical serialization for signatures or rely on authenticated transport plus signed/validated protocol envelopes as appropriate. Define replay protection, maximum timestamp skew, message size bounds, JSON schema validation, careful URL encoding, DNS/URL allow policies where appropriate, and per-device origin authorization. The parser must emit supported intent ENUMS and typed arguments. NEVER convert free-form AI text directly into `cmd.exe`, PowerShell, Bash, AppleScript or a generic arbitrary terminal command. Privileged or open-ended shell execution is outside the default assistant scope and should require explicit specialized developer tools, an allowlisted workspace, and higher review. Remember that URL search queries must be encoded, not concatenated unsafely into system shell commands.

Response protocol:
```json
{
  "request_id": "uuid",
  "target_device_id": "paired-desktop-id",
  "status": "success|partial|requires_approval|denied|unsupported|expired|failed",
  "action": "OPEN_WEB_SEARCH",
  "verified_facts": ["Browser open request accepted by operating system"],
  "result": {"opened_url": "https://www.google.com/search?q=ChatGPT"},
  "error": null,
  "duration_ms": 0,
  "receipt_id": "uuid"
}
```
Distinguish "OS accepted open URL" from "page fully loaded", and "app process launched" from "task inside app finished". Only claim the strongest success actually observed. Add optional agent `progress` events and user-visible `cancel` support. Track target device, privilege tier, required scope, idempotency, user confirmation, OS constraints, localization, result, and reason for failure. If device is offline, commands must expire instead of executing hours later unexpectedly unless the user specifically schedules a safe deferred action.

## 1.6 Windows desktop adapter
Use default protocol handlers to open HTTPS search URLs, the Windows ShellExecute family or framework-appropriate safe launcher APIs to start registered apps, and Windows UI Automation when the user has enabled targeted UI interactions. Microsoft UI Automation is suited to discovering app control patterns for accessible UI; do not inject input into secure desktop, UAC prompts, password fields, protected apps, or another user's session. Separate current user session capabilities from elevated administrator tasks. Use Windows-known folders APIs or granted directories rather than assuming path layouts. Treat installed app discovery as a per-user scoped listing. User-friendly failure examples: "Chrome is not installed; should I use your default browser?" and "The folder isn't authorized yet; choose it on your computer." Prefer OS-controlled display of sensitive approval dialogs. Package using signed installer when credentials are available; support EXE and MSI/MSIX as appropriate, add uninstall/start menu integration and auto-updater with cryptographic signature checks.

## 1.7 macOS desktop adapter
Use NSWorkspace or approved URL-opening APIs, LaunchServices for registered apps, sandbox-consistent file selection and security-scoped bookmarks if relevant, and user-approved Accessibility/Apple Events permissions only for supported app automation. Respect TCC permission prompts; never try to bypass prompts, silently grant accessibility or simulate security-sensitive user actions. Provide visible menu-bar app and pairing controls. Explain App Store vs notarized direct distribution, Hardened Runtime and code-signing requirements. The default voice route remains the Android phone; macOS can offer its own optional audio input/output when present, but desktop voice is never required. Test permissions and behavior across macOS versions and Apple Silicon/Intel targets that are supported by the build pipeline.

## 1.8 Linux desktop adapter
Use `xdg-open` or documented desktop portals for launching URLs and opening files. For remote desktop input and screenshots on Wayland, prefer XDG Desktop Portal RemoteDesktop/ScreenCast with user-visible session approval when actually needed; do not promise arbitrary desktop control without user consent. Support X11 and Wayland differences explicitly, GNOME/KDE variations, desktop environment limitations, systemd user service where suitable, and formats such as AppImage, .deb, .rpm, or a distro-specific package when feasible. No blanket root permissions or hidden keylogging. Test Ubuntu LTS GNOME and a KDE Wayland configuration as practical smoke-test baselines. If the graphical session is absent (SSH-only machine), report that GUI opening may not be available.

## 1.9 Cross-platform action catalog with concrete results
`DEVICE_PING`, `GET_DEVICE_INFO`, `OPEN_APP`, `OPEN_URL`, `OPEN_WEB_SEARCH`, `FOCUS_WINDOW`, `LIST_RUNNING_APPS` when permitted, `OPEN_APPROVED_FOLDER`, `SEARCH_APPROVED_FOLDER`, `OPEN_SELECTED_FILE`, `MEDIA_PLAY_PAUSE`, `MEDIA_NEXT`, `SET_APP_VOLUME` when supported, `SHOW_NOTIFICATION`, `OPEN_CODE_WORKSPACE`, `COPY_TEXT_TO_APPROVED_CLIPBOARD`, `LAUNCH_USER_DEFINED_SHORTCUT`, `GET_ACTIVE_WINDOW_TITLE` when permitted, `GET_POWER_STATUS`, `START_SAFE_FOCUS_TIMER`, `DISPLAY_AI_ANSWER`, `REQUEST_SCREENSHOT_APPROVAL`, `REQUEST_FILE_READ_APPROVAL`, `CANCEL_JOB`, `GET_JOB_STATUS`, `DISCONNECT_DEVICE`, `REVOKE_PAIRING`. Each action has a request schema, supported target platforms, required scopes, offline support, OS adapters, success verification, retry/idempotence, risk tier, user-facing confirmation, and end-to-end test. Only add more actions after threat-model and feasibility review. Prefer user-defined workflows with tightly constrained inputs over arbitrary agent control.

For the primary user scenario, `OPEN_WEB_SEARCH` should choose a browser using a registered app identifier, escape the search query through a URL encoder, open an HTTPS search URL with the OS launcher, optionally confirm window/process visibility when OS permissions allow, then send completion status. If the user specifically says "Chrome", prefer Chrome if installed, otherwise ask permission to use the default browser. Do not rely on screenshots/clicking when a stable URL API exists. Do not attempt to silently manipulate another person's desktop without authorized pairing.

## 1.10 Cross-device session intelligence
Allow a selected default computer, discover multiple paired devices, show per-device OS, battery or power status if exposed, connection mode, name, last seen, latency, capabilities, and permission state. Remember only the user's chosen friendly name and verified device ID, not nearby strangers' computer details. Support pronouns and follow-ups: "Open VS Code on the laptop" then "Search the web for Kotlin coroutines on that same computer"; "Use the Mac instead" updates the target; "Stop" aborts pending operations, but cannot undo side effects already performed. Distinguish context "on my phone" versus "on my computer". Provide a visible target badge and verbal disambiguation when multiple devices could respond. User must be able to suspend desktop access instantly from either device.

## 1.11 Quality, network resilience and scheduling
Implement heartbeat/presence checks, exponential reconnect with jitter, local LAN fallback after cloud relay failure if trust remains valid, selectable quality mode, message serialization version negotiation, minimal persistent queue, observability without raw user speech logs, cancellation tokens, and clock-skew handling. Build an integration test rig with network loss, Wi-Fi handoff, router isolation, firewall block, desktop sleep, user logout, bridge restart, OS upgrade, revoked permission, expired token, app crash, phone low battery, and device key rotation. Mark stale device presence honestly. A reconnect must never replay a destructive task; use idempotency and action receipts. For asynchronous safe tasks, allow explicit schedule, expiry, and scope. For destructive or external tasks, require fresh confirmation on execution.

## 1.12 Installer and delivery requirements
Build self-contained desktop companions for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Windows: EXE/MSI/MSIX depending selected stack and deployment channel. macOS: signed/notarized DMG/PKG when developer credentials allow. Linux: AppImage or native packages depending compatibility. Use GitHub Actions matrix on real OS runners to produce reproducible build artifacts, checksums, software bill of materials, provenance when feasible, and security scan reports. Documentation must explain development vs production signing, warning dialogs for unsigned installers, GitHub Release artifact publishing, no guarantee that bare executables are trusted by operating systems, and verification of downloaded installer checksums. Do not pretend a Linux binary built on Windows is tested on every distribution. Windows/macOS/Linux installs are separate client packages sharing the protocol and backend.

## 1.13 Contextual conversation examples that MUST work
- User: "Hey JARVIS." Phone: "Hello, sir. How can I help you?" Keep answer optional and personalizable.
- User: "Open Chrome on my PC." Assistant verifies target and app and replies after receipt: "Chrome is open on your Windows computer."
- User: "Search ChatGPT." Using last target, bridge opens a safely encoded browser search. Phone: "I started the ChatGPT search on that computer."
- User: "What does my screen show?" App: "I can ask your computer to share a screenshot. Approve it on the computer first." Only then capture and analyze.
- User: "Read the private folder on the desktop." App: "That folder isn't shared with J.A.R.V.I.S. Choose the folder and grant access on the computer."
- User: "Install the latest Python on my computer." App: "I can open the official Python download page or prepare instructions. Software installation requires your review and system permissions."
- User: "Send Mom that I'm coming home." Assistant resolves contact, displays the message preview, asks user for confirmation, and reports delivery status only if the messaging provider confirms it.
- User: "Stop listening." Mic off immediately with a visible state change; no passive recording.
- User: "How can you hear me when the computer doesn't have a microphone?" Response: "Your phone captures your voice. The paired desktop receives only the commands and approved data it needs; your computer does not need its own microphone."

## 1.14 Threat model: remote control must NEVER become an unbounded remote-access trojan
Attack surfaces include local-network impostors, malicious QR codes, stolen phones, intercepted relay traffic, replayed commands, prompt injection in documents/webpages, compromised cloud tokens, malicious skill manifests, desktop accessibility permission escalation, inherited admin privileges, dangerous user-installed plugins, accidental disclosure through logs, and overly broad file grants. Apply defense in depth: mutual authentication, certificate/key verification, authenticated transport, signed client updates, capability scopes, local human approval, expiration, command schemas, trusted channel verification, secure token storage, replay detection, policy engine, auditing, identity revocation, and a global stop button. Lock all default capabilities to harmless initial tasks. Deny any remote operation outside the granted list. No silent background audio recording, hidden screen capture, stealth persistence, password extraction, keylogging, arbitrary shell access, credential harvesting, circumvented lock screens, or unauthorized access to someone else's computer. Document how to disable and uninstall all components.

## 1.15 Live voice is an active user feature, not surveillance
The user's phrase "listen everything" must be interpreted as "understand my requests robustly during sessions I choose to activate," not "record everyone continuously." Wake-word recognition, if feasible, should be locally evaluated, user-configured, visually disclosed, and OS-policy compliant. Don't guarantee performance beyond the phone's physical microphone. Improve real-world intelligibility using audio source selection, gain calibration where permitted, noise suppression, echo cancellation, VAD, language detection, STT context vocabulary and low-latency interruptible TTS. Record no raw audio by default, and never record other people's calls or private conversations without appropriate consent and platform support. Microphone hardware and background restrictions are real and cannot be overridden by a prompt.
